title: Hypoglycaemia & diabetic emergencies
blurb: Recognise a hypo early, treat it with oral glucose or glucagon, and know how hyperglycaemia differs.
question: A patient with type 1 diabetes skipped breakfast to get to her early appointment. Halfway through a scale and polish she becomes sweaty, shaky and unusually snappy, and her speech is muddled. What is the likely cause, and what should you give her?

teach.h: Too little or too much glucose
teach.body: The brain runs on glucose. People with diabetes who take insulin or some tablets can have their blood glucose drop too low: hypoglycaemia, a 'hypo', usually below 4 mmol/L. A hypo comes on fast, over minutes, and is the diabetic emergency you are most likely to see in practice. Common causes are a missed or late meal (often skipped before an appointment), too much insulin, extra exercise or alcohol. Hyperglycaemia, blood glucose that is too high, develops slowly over hours or days.

teach.h: Treating a hypo: one question decides

children.label: Oral glucose 15–20 g
children.sub: Gel, sugary drink or tablets; recheck in 15 min

items: Stop treatment and sit the patient up. Reassure them.
Give 15–20 g of fast-acting glucose by mouth: glucose gel, a sugary (non-diet) drink, glucose tablets or sugar lumps.
Recheck after 15 minutes. If they are not improving, repeat the glucose.
Once they feel better, give longer-acting carbohydrate (a sandwich or biscuits) so the glucose doesn't drop again.
Monitor until fully recovered. The dentist decides whether treatment continues, and the patient should not drive away straight afterwards.

head: Drug
Dose
Route
When
teach.caption: Children: oral glucose 5 g (up to 5 yrs), 10 g (5–11 yrs), 15 g (12–17 yrs). Glucagon 0.5 mg for ages 2–8 or under 25 kg; 1 mg for ages 9 and over or 25 kg and over (SDCEP).

teach.h: How glucagon works, and its limits
teach.body: Glucagon is a hormone that tells the liver to release its stored glucose into the blood. That means it works poorly if the liver has little stored glucose, for example after a long fast or heavy drinking. It takes some minutes to act, so keep the patient in the recovery position and call 999. Once they wake and can swallow, give oral glucose and then a starchy snack. Never pour food or drink into the mouth of an unconscious patient: they could choke.

items.label: then recheck and repeat if needed

teach.body: High blood glucose builds slowly, so it rarely appears suddenly in the chair. Look for thirst, passing a lot of urine, tiredness and drowsiness, nausea, and a fruity, 'pear drops' smell on the breath with deep, rapid breathing, which suggests diabetic ketoacidosis. This patient needs urgent medical assessment: call 999 if they are very drowsy or unwell. The dental team never gives insulin.

teach.text: Not sure if a conscious diabetic patient is hypo or hyper? Give glucose. A little extra sugar won't harm someone with high glucose in the short term, but an untreated hypo can cause a seizure or unconsciousness within minutes. Also, don't mistake a hypo for rudeness or drunkenness.

items: Hypo: fast onset; shaky, sweaty, pale, irritable, confused; often a missed meal.
Conscious and can swallow: oral glucose 15–20 g, recheck at 15 minutes, then a starchy snack.
Unconscious or can't swallow: glucagon 1 mg IM, recovery position, call 999.
Hyper: slow onset; thirst, passing urine, drowsy, fruity breath: urgent medical help.
If in doubt in a conscious patient, give glucose.

summary: You can now tell a hypo from a hyper, treat a conscious hypo with oral glucose and follow-up carbohydrate, give glucagon 1 mg IM to a patient who can't swallow, and recognise hyperglycaemia as a reason for urgent medical help.

A.q: A diabetic patient who missed lunch becomes sweaty, shaky and confused during treatment. What is the most likely cause?
A.why: Sweating, trembling and confusion that come on quickly after a missed meal are classic signs of a hypo.

whyNot.0: Hyperglycaemia develops slowly and causes thirst and drowsiness rather than sweating.
whyNot.1: A faint causes pallor and brief loss of consciousness, usually with a trigger like a needle, and recovers when flat.
whyNot.2: Hyperventilation causes fast breathing and tingling, not low-glucose signs.

A.q: A conscious patient with a suspected hypo can swallow safely. What should you give?
A.why: A conscious patient who can swallow is given 15–20 g of fast-acting oral glucose, such as glucose gel or a sugary drink.

whyNot.0: Glucagon is for a patient who is unconscious or can't swallow.
whyNot.2: Aspirin is for suspected heart attack.
whyNot.3: Insulin lowers glucose further and could be fatal in a hypo.

A.q: A diabetic patient becomes unconscious and is breathing. A hypo is suspected. Which drug is given?
options: Glucose gel squeezed into the mouth
A sugary drink poured into the mouth
A.why: An unconscious patient can't swallow safely, so glucagon 1 mg is given IM, with the patient in the recovery position and 999 called.

whyNot.0: Putting gel in an unconscious patient's mouth risks choking.
whyNot.1: Pouring liquid into the mouth of an unconscious patient risks choking and aspiration.
whyNot.3: Midazolam treats prolonged seizures, not low glucose.

B.q: A diabetic patient says she has been very thirsty and passing a lot of urine for days. She is drowsy and her breath smells fruity. What does this suggest?
B.why: Thirst, passing lots of urine, drowsiness and fruity breath developing over days point to high glucose, possibly ketoacidosis.

whyNot.0: A hypo comes on in minutes with sweating, shaking and confusion.
whyNot.2: Anaphylaxis is sudden, with rash, swelling, wheeze or collapse after a trigger.
whyNot.3: Angina causes chest pain, not thirst or fruity breath.

B.q: A patient recovers well after oral glucose for a hypo. What should happen next?
options: Give a starchy snack and monitor
B.why: Longer-acting carbohydrate stops the glucose dropping again, and the patient is monitored until fully recovered.

whyNot.0: She could have another hypo if sent away without food and monitoring.
whyNot.1: Glucagon is only for a patient who can't swallow; she has already recovered.
whyNot.3: She needs time to recover fully before the dentist decides on treatment.

B.q: After giving 15–20 g of oral glucose, when should you recheck and consider a repeat dose?
B.why: SDCEP advises repeating oral glucose after 15 minutes if the patient hasn't improved.

whyNot.0: Two minutes is too soon for glucose to take effect.
whyNot.2: An hour is far too long to leave a hypo untreated.
whyNot.3: Waiting for collapse lets a hypo worsen dangerously.

C.q: A conscious diabetic patient is unwell, and you can't tell whether it's a hypo or a hyper. What is the safest action?
C.why: If in doubt, treat as a hypo. Extra sugar won't harm a hyper patient in the short term, but an untreated hypo can quickly become dangerous.

whyNot.0: The dental team never gives insulin, and it could be fatal in a hypo.
whyNot.1: Waiting lets a hypo progress to seizure or unconsciousness.
whyNot.2: GTN treats angina and has no role here.

C.q: Why might glucagon work poorly in a patient who has been fasting for a long time?
options: It must be given with salbutamol
C.why: Glucagon works by releasing glucose stored in the liver, so it is less effective when those stores are depleted.

whyNot.1: Glucagon is given by IM injection, not by mouth.
whyNot.2: Salbutamol is an asthma reliever and has nothing to do with glucagon.
whyNot.3: Fasting doesn't affect the injection site; it affects the liver's glucose stores.

C.q: Which of these is NOT a usual cause of a hypo in a patient taking insulin?
options: Running to the surgery when late
C.why: A large sugary meal raises blood glucose. Missed meals, eating less than planned and extra exercise all cause hypos.

whyNot.0: Missing a meal is one of the commonest causes of a hypo.
whyNot.2: Insulin without enough food lowers glucose too far.
whyNot.3: Unplanned exercise uses up glucose and can cause a hypo.

reteach.title: The fuel gauge
reteach.question: Think of the brain as an engine that only runs on one fuel: glucose. What happens as the tank runs dry, and how do you refuel it?

blocks.body: In a hypo the fuel gauge drops fast. First the body sounds the alarm: shaking, sweating, a racing heart, hunger. Then the brain itself starts to falter: confusion, odd or aggressive behaviour, slurred speech. Leave it and the engine cuts out: seizure or unconsciousness. If the patient can still swallow, top up the tank by mouth. If they can't, glucagon makes the liver release its reserve tank.

steps.label: Missed meal or too much insulin

blocks.caption: Treat at the earliest stage: oral glucose while they can swallow, glucagon 1 mg IM once they can't.

explain.body: A hypo comes on in minutes: pale, sweaty, shaky, hungry, irritable or aggressive, confused. Ask whether the patient has eaten and taken their usual medication.

test.q: A usually calm diabetic patient suddenly becomes rude, sweaty and confused. What should you suspect first?
test.why: Sudden behaviour change with sweating and confusion in a diabetic patient is a hypo until proven otherwise.

whyNot.0: Hyperventilation causes fast breathing and tingling, not sweating with confusion.
whyNot.2: Hypos are often mistaken for drunkenness; treat the hypo.
whyNot.3: A panic attack doesn't explain confusion in a diabetic patient.

explain.body: 15–20 g of fast-acting glucose (gel, sugary drink, tablets). Recheck at 15 minutes and repeat if needed, then give a starchy snack.

test.q: Which is a suitable fast-acting glucose source for a conscious hypo?
test.why: Glucose gel is absorbed quickly. A sandwich comes afterwards as the longer-acting carbohydrate.

whyNot.1: A sandwich is too slow on its own; it follows the fast glucose.
whyNot.3: Milk contains some sugar but is not a fast-acting glucose source.

explain.body: Nothing by mouth. Give glucagon 1 mg IM (0.5 mg for ages 2–8 or under 25 kg), place in the recovery position and call 999. Give oral glucose once the patient wakes and can swallow.

test.q: What dose of glucagon is given IM to an unconscious adult with a hypo?
test.why: Adults and children aged 9 and over (or 25 kg and over) receive glucagon 1 mg IM.

whyNot.0: 0.5 mg is the dose for children aged 2–8 or under 25 kg.
whyNot.1: 10 mg is the adult dose of buccal midazolam, not glucagon.
whyNot.3: 15 g is an oral glucose amount, not a glucagon dose.

explain.body: Slow onset over hours or days: thirst, passing lots of urine, drowsiness, fruity breath, deep breathing. Needs urgent medical help; the dental team doesn't give insulin.

test.q: Which sign points to hyperglycaemia rather than a hypo?
test.why: A fruity smell on the breath suggests ketones from very high glucose (ketoacidosis).

whyNot.0: Sudden sweating is typical of a hypo.
whyNot.2: Trembling is a hypo warning sign.
whyNot.3: Rapid onset is typical of a hypo; hyperglycaemia builds slowly.
